newsitem.title: THAILAND: INTERVIEW - MDX to build second Laos plant.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - MDX to build second Laos plant.

text.p: MDX Power Co Ltd said on Wednesday it has decided to build a second hydro-power plant in Laos, despite several failed talks on electricity pricing with its main buyer, Thailand's state-run electricity authority.
Swarng Champa, managing director of MDX Power, a subsidiary of MDX Plc, told Reuters in an interview that total investment in the plant would be $680 million.
MDX Power would hold 55 percent of the total capital while the remainder would be held by the Laotian government, Swarng said.
"MDX Power plans to borrow 70 percent of the total funds from the Asian Development Bank or from any local or foreign commercial bank."

The plant will have a production capacity of 440 megawatts and the company wants to sell 95 percent of the output to the Electricity Generating Authority of Thailand (EGAT) and the rest to Laos, he said.
Swarng said the company was still negotiating with EGAT but hoped to settle pricing problems within the next six months.
"EGAT has proposed buying power from the second plant at a price of five cents per unit in 2003 and our company has asked for more," he said.
Construction is expected to start next year. The plant will take about six years to complete and will be located about 170 kms northeast of the Laotian capital of Vientiane.

MDX Power's first $280 million hydro-power plant, which has a production capacity of 210 megawatts and is located near the Nam Hinboun River, is a joint venture project between MDX Power, state-enterprise Electricite de Laos and Norway's Nordic Hydro-power AB.
The Laotian side holds 60 percent while MDX Power and Nordic Hydro-power each own 20 percent.
Under an agreement, MDX Power will sell power from the first plant at 4.85 cents per unit starting from March 1998 with annual price increases during the first 10 years.
Established nearly five years ago, MDX Power is now conducting feasibility studies to establish power plants in Burma near the Thai border and in the southern Chinese province of Yunnan, Swarng said.

"If approved by the Burmese government, the hydro-power project, which could generate a maximum of 200 megawatts, would be the first cross-border plant. I believe that the parties involved in this feasibility study need to be patient in dealing with the Burmese government," he said.

At least 40 million baht ($1.6 million) is needed for the feasibility study in the Burmese project, he said. The company and Thai major construction firm Italian-Thai Development Plc will each foot 35 percent of the bill while Japan's Marubeni Corp will pay the rest.

"The feasibility study to build a hydro-power plant in Yunnan which could generate up to 1,500 megawatts is expected to be completed late next year. Construction could start in 2000 and it would take about six years to complete if the project is approved by the Chinese government," Swarng said.
